headline: A record heat wave hits the United States

sources.title: US heat wave death toll grows
19 deaths in New Jersey likely connected to heat wave, officials say
Heat-related deaths mount after historic Fourth of July heat wave broiled eastern US

chunks.text: A dangerous [[heat wave]] {{heated up}} much of the United States over the July 4 holiday weekend. A large [[heat dome]] settled over the country, and the extreme heat {{set in}} from the Midwest to the East Coast. Officials said about 40 million people were under a [[heat alert]] on Sunday. Weather forecasters warned of a serious danger to people's health.

verbs.wrong: To stay hot for many days
To spread quickly from place to place
verbs.correct: To begin and seem likely to continue

chunks.text: Forecasters said the heat wave broke many old records. Temperatures {{shot up}} above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many cities. In Washington, D.C., the [[temperature]] reached 103 degrees on July 4, which officials said was a new [[record]]. High [[humidity]] made the air feel even hotter. Overnight, the air did not {{cool down}} much, and the low stayed near 80 degrees, so many people could not {{cool off}}.

verbs.wrong: To stay at a very high level
To take a rest in the shade

chunks.text: Officials said the heat wave was blamed for at least 24 deaths across the country during the week. In New Jersey, state health officials said about 22 deaths were linked to the heat. They {{pointed out}} that extreme heat is one of the deadliest kinds of weather in the United States. Officials asked people to {{look out for}} older neighbors and anyone living without [[air conditioning]].

verbs.correct: To tell someone a fact they may not know
To take care to protect someone

chunks.text: To help people {{deal with}} the heat, many cities opened a [[cooling center]] where residents could stay cool. Officials asked people to {{carry on}} drinking water and to rest indoors during the hottest hours. Some outdoor events were {{called off}} for safety. By early the next week, forecasters said the heat would finally {{let up}} as cooler air moved in.

verbs.wrong: To stay away from something dangerous
verbs.correct: To take action to solve a problem

verbs.wrong: To remember to do something important
To move an event indoors for safety
To move away to a different region

ex: The kitchen began to heat up as she cooked dinner.
The whole region will heat up again later this week.
By noon, the city had heated up to over 100 degrees.

vocab.def: To begin and seem likely to continue
ex: The cold weather set in early that winter.
Once the heat set in, it stayed for many days.
Tiredness set in after the long trip.
Prices shot up after the shortage began.
The temperature shot up in just a few hours.
His fever shot up during the night.
The soup needs a few minutes to cool down.
The air finally cooled down after sunset.
Open a window to help the room cool down.
The children jumped in the pool to cool off.
She sat in the shade to cool off after her run.
People used fans to cool off during the heat wave.

vocab.def: To tell someone a fact they may not know
ex: The teacher pointed out a mistake in my essay.
She pointed out that the store was already closed.
Experts pointed out that heat can be very dangerous.

vocab.def: To take care to protect someone
ex: Please look out for your little brother at the park.
Neighbors looked out for each other during the storm.
Officials asked people to look out for older residents.

vocab.def: To take action to solve a problem
ex: The city worked hard to deal with the flooding.
We need a plan to deal with the extra traffic.
It is not easy to deal with such high temperatures.
They carried on working even when it got dark.
Please carry on; I did not mean to interrupt.
Officials asked people to carry on drinking water.
The team called off the game because of the storm.
They called off the trip when the weather got worse.
Some outdoor events were called off for safety.
The rain did not let up all afternoon.
The heat finally let up when cooler air arrived.
The wind began to let up in the evening.

wordDefs.def: A long period of very hot weather
ex: The heat wave lasted for more than a week.
Many people stayed indoors during the heat wave.

wordDefs.def: A large area of high pressure that traps hot air over a region
ex: A heat dome sat over the country for several days.
The heat dome brought record temperatures to the East Coast.

wordDefs.def: An official warning that dangerous heat is expected
ex: The city issued a heat alert for the weekend.
Millions of people were under a heat alert on Sunday.

wordDefs.def: How hot or cold something is
ex: The temperature reached 103 degrees on July 4.
Nurses checked the patient's temperature every hour.

wordDefs.def: The highest or best level ever measured
ex: The city set a new heat record that day.
Officials said the old record had stood for many years.

wordDefs.def: The amount of water in the air
ex: High humidity made the hot day feel even worse.
The humidity dropped once the storm passed.

wordDefs.def: A system that cools the air inside a building or car
ex: Their apartment did not have air conditioning.
The store kept its air conditioning on all day.

wordDefs.def: A public place where people can go to stay cool
ex: The library was used as a cooling center during the heat wave.
Officials asked people without air conditioning to visit a cooling center.

tf.s: Overnight, the air did not cool down much, and the low stayed near 80 degrees.
tf.why: Correct. The air did not cool down, which means it did not become cooler; the low stayed near 80 degrees.

tf.s: The extreme heat cooled off from the Midwest to the East Coast.
tf.why: The correct verb is set in. The heat began and continued across the region; it did not cool off, which would mean become less hot.

tf.s: Temperatures let up above 100 degrees Fahrenheit in many cities.
tf.why: The correct verb is shot up. Temperatures rose quickly above 100 degrees; let up would mean they became less strong.

tf.s: Over the holiday weekend, a heat wave heated up much of the United States.
tf.why: Correct. The heat wave heated up (made much hotter) large parts of the country. Heat up means to become or make something hotter.

tf.s: Some outdoor events were called off for safety.
tf.why: Correct. The events were called off, which means they were canceled for safety.

tf.s: Officials asked people to call off drinking water during the heat.
tf.why: The correct verb is carry on. Officials asked people to continue drinking water; call off would mean to cancel it.
